article_blocks.text: Strain Type: 75% Indica / 25% Sativa
Genetics: Selected phenotype of Girl Scout Cookies
Breeder: Burning Bush Nurseries
THC Content: 19–27%
CBD Content: Typically very low
Terpene Profile: Myrcene , limonene , beta-caryophyllene
Primary Flavors: Lime candy, citrus zest, mint
Flowering Time (Indoor): 9–10 weeks
Outdoor Harvest Time: early to mid-October
Indoor Yield: 300–400 g/m²
Outdoor Yield: 350–400 g per plant
Grow Difficulty: Moderate

Key Lime Pie is one of the rare cannabis strains whose dessert name captures only half of what is happening in the flower. Fresh buds can release an unmistakable burst of lime zest and sugary citrus, yet beneath that brightness sit cool mint, vanilla cream, earthy chocolate, pepper, and the unmistakable doughy funk of the Cookies family . The cultivar emerged during the early expansion of Girl Scout Cookies genetics in California, when growers were discovering that individual GSC phenotypes could express dramatically different aromas and growth characteristics.

The plant most commonly identified as the classic Key Lime Pie was selected for unusually strong lime terpenes, dense resin production, purple-tinted flower, and an indica-leaning high. Phylos Bioscience’s preserved oral history likewise identifies the Burning Bush Nurseries plant as a distinctive GSC phenotype selected for lime candy, mint, spice, earth, and chocolate characteristics. Modern cultivation shows that it can also be considerably stronger than early examples, with current flower testing around 27% THC in some regulated markets.
Genetics and Lineage

The most accurate genetic description is not a conventional two-parent cross but a selected phenotype of Girl Scout Cookies. Burning Bush Nurseries is widely associated with the clone that established the familiar Key Lime Pie identity, while another California breeder, Purple Caper Seeds, developed a separate seed version from GSC material. This distinction matters because the name now appears on several products and seed lines that are not necessarily genetically identical. Phylos records the Burning Bush version specifically as a gourmet GSC phenotype rather than an independent GSC × Lime strain.

The broader GSC family is commonly associated with OG Kush and Durban -derived ancestry, providing a useful explanation for the cultivar’s mixture of dense resinous flower and brighter citrus-spice characteristics. The OG side contributes compact flower formation, fuel, earth, and substantial physical effects, while Durban-related influence helps preserve more cerebral energy and sharp aromatic complexity. Within that genetic population, Key Lime Pie stands apart because the citrus expression became dramatically more specific: not generic lemon, but something closer to lime peel, lime candy, and creamy citrus pie.

A separate Purple Caper Seeds lineage adds another layer to the history. That breeder reportedly worked a Santa Cruz GSC clone back into GSC F2 material to make a reproducible seed population with similar lime-and-mint traits. The two versions are therefore related through GSC but should not automatically be treated as the exact same plant. For a strain library , identifying the classic Burning Bush-associated cultivar as a selected GSC phenotype is more precise than inventing a separate Lime OG parent that does not appear in the better-documented historical record.
Effects and Experience

The experience often begins faster than its indica-dominant classification suggests. An initial cerebral shift can bring euphoria, greater sensory interest, and a pleasantly creative quality while leaving the consumer mentally aware of what is happening around them. Conversation, movies, music, or quiet creative activities can fit the first part of the high particularly well. Rather than producing frantic stimulation, the mental effect tends to feel lucid and warm.

Physical relaxation becomes more important as the session develops. The body can begin to feel noticeably heavier while the earlier mental brightness remains partially intact, producing an unusual combination of couch-friendly comfort and cerebral clarity. Higher amounts push the cultivar much further toward sedation, which explains why some consumers view this weed as an evening strain despite its relatively engaging opening. The sweet lime flavor can disguise its strength, making it easy to consume more before the first serving has fully developed.

Potency varies substantially between growers. A current regulated flower profile from River Valley Relief lists 27.3% THC, 28.4% total cannabinoids, and 1.8% total terpenes. Other preserved descriptions place typical flower closer to the low-to-mid 20% range. For consumers with limited tolerance, strong examples can produce dry mouth, red eyes, dizziness, temporary anxiety, impaired coordination, or pronounced drowsiness when the dose becomes excessive.
Medical Benefits

Medical marijuana consumers may be interested in the strain because its effects combine mental uplift with increasingly substantial physical relaxation. Some people may prefer this pattern when everyday stress and bodily tension occur together: the cerebral phase can remain relatively pleasant and engaged, while the later portion of the high encourages rest and physical comfort. Larger doses tend to favor evening use because sedation becomes increasingly likely.

Those experiences should not be interpreted as evidence that Key Lime Pie treats pain, anxiety, insomnia, depression, or another medical disorder. Named cannabis cultivars are chemically variable, and the same genetic label can represent very different THC and terpene concentrations from one grow to another. Anyone using weed medicinally should give more weight to the laboratory results of the specific product, dosage, personal response, medication interactions, and guidance from an appropriate healthcare professional.
Flavor Profile and Aroma

Lime is the unmistakable signature. Intact buds can smell like sweet citrus candy or freshly grated lime peel, while breaking the flower apart exposes mint, pepper, earth, and a deeper cookie-like funk. Heat changes the profile again: the brighter citrus can give way to vanilla, chocolate, toasted dough, and spice. That transition is one reason the strain earned a separate identity despite emerging from GSC—it does not simply smell like a slightly more citrus-forward Cookies phenotype.

Laboratory data demonstrates how variable the chemistry can be while preserving the same overall flavor theme. River Valley Relief currently reports myrcene at 0.56%, limonene at 0.33%, linalool at 0.28%, beta-caryophyllene at 0.27%, and humulene at 0.12% in its flower. A 2025 concentrate analysis from another producer was instead led by limonene at 1.58%, followed by beta-caryophyllene and myrcene, with pinene and linalool also present. These differences show why the cultivar may lean more toward ripe fruit in one harvest and sharper lime or pepper in another.

The inhale generally emphasizes lime candy, citrus, and mild sweetness. Mint and cream develop through the middle, while earth, black pepper, chocolate, and Cookies-like dough remain after the exhale. Proper curing is especially important because the volatile citrus notes can disappear rapidly when flower is overdried or stored in excessive heat.
Growing Information

Key Lime Pie generally develops as a compact-to-medium plant with heavy resin production and dense flowering sites. The classic Burning Bush-associated material is documented with a flowering period of approximately 63–70 days, placing most indoor plants in a nine-to-ten-week window. Preserved nursery material similarly places indoor production around 300–400 g/m² and describes the cultivar as intermediate in difficulty, with moderate stretch and strong lateral branching.

Topping during vegetative growth can help spread branches across a wider footprint, while low-stress training or a trellis improves light distribution as flowering stretch begins. The plant’s compact Cookies-style flowers can become extremely resinous toward maturity, so adequate airflow is particularly important through the center of the canopy. Selective removal of weak interior growth can reduce crowding without excessively stripping productive leaves.

Purple coloration can become more obvious late in bloom, particularly when nighttime temperatures naturally decline. The classic cultivar is known for green flowers that can develop purple highlights beneath heavy trichome coverage. Outdoor growers generally aim for an early-to-mid-October finish in suitable Northern Hemisphere climates. Because the buds become dense, regions with prolonged autumn rain can be more challenging than dry Mediterranean-style conditions.
FAQ
What are the genetics of Key Lime Pie?

The classic Key Lime Pie is best documented as a selected phenotype of Girl Scout Cookies rather than a completely separate hybrid. Burning Bush Nurseries is widely associated with the famous clone, while Purple Caper Seeds later developed a separate GSC-based seed version.
Is Key Lime Pie indica or sativa?

It is generally considered an indica-dominant hybrid, often described around 75% indica and 25% sativa. The experience can initially feel cerebral and creative before stronger body relaxation and potential drowsiness develop.
How strong is Key Lime Pie?

Potency commonly falls somewhere in the 19–27% THC range in modern flower. A current regulated example tested at 27.3% THC. Actual strength varies by phenotype, cultivation, harvest maturity, and laboratory methodology.
What does Key Lime Pie taste like?
Lime candy and citrus zest dominate the beginning, accompanied by mint and sweetness. Vanilla cream, earthy spice, chocolate, pepper, and cookie dough become more apparent during the finish.
How long does Key Lime Pie take to flower?

The classic cultivar typically requires about nine to ten weeks indoors, with historical Burning Bush material placed around 63–70 days. Outdoor plants generally mature in early to mid-October under favorable Northern Hemisphere conditions.
Final Thoughts on Key Lime Pie

Key Lime Pie demonstrates how a single phenotype can become almost as influential as a newly created cross. The plant began inside the Girl Scout Cookies family, yet selection for sharp lime aromatics, purple-tinted resinous flowers, and a heavier indica expression gave it enough personality to become a recognized cultivar in its own right. Preserved genetic history continues to identify the classic Burning Bush-associated plant as a gourmet GSC phenotype rather than a generic lime-flavored hybrid.

Its lasting appeal comes from contrast. Lime candy and mint make the first impression bright and almost refreshing, but chocolate, earth, pepper, cream, and Cookies-like dough provide a darker finish. The high follows the same progression, moving from cerebral euphoria and creative clarity toward deeper physical relaxation. Add THC potential well into the 20% range, heavy resin production, and a manageable nine-to-ten-week flowering cycle, and Key Lime Pie remains one of the more distinctive expressions to emerge from the enormously influential Cookies family.
